title: Episode 99: The Republic of Vermont: Fourteen Years of Independence (1777–1791)
description:
Between 1777 and 1791, before joining the United States as the fourteenth state, Vermont existed as an independent, self-governing sovereign republic with its own postal system, copper currency, army, and the first constitution in North America to abolish slavery.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we delve into one of the most astonishing and overlooked political anomalies in American history: the fourteen-year saga of the independent Republic of Vermont. Long before it became the fourteen state of the Union in seventeen ninety-one, Vermont was not a British colony, nor was it recognized as one of the original thirteen United States. Denied statehood by the Continental Congress due to territory claims by New York and New Hampshire, Vermont's bold settlers declared themselves an independent nation in January seventeen seventy-seven. For fourteen years, this mountain republic minted its own copper coins, ran its own postal service, fielded its own army, and enacted the most progressive constitution in human history—the first in the Western Hemisphere to outlaw adult slavery and grant universal male suffrage without property qualifications. Here is George with the full, fascinating chronicle.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: CAUGHT BETWEEN NEW YORK AND NEW HAMPSHIRE
To understand why Vermont became an independent republic rather than an ordinary state, one must look at the tangled legal web of colonial New England land speculation. In the mid-eighteenth century, Royal Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire began aggressively selling off one hundred and thirty-one township charters in the wilderness west of the Connecticut River, pocketing handsome fees and reserving five hundred acres in every township for himself. Settlers from Massachusetts and Connecticut cleared the dense forests, planted corn, and built communities, assuming their New Hampshire land titles were unimpeachable.
However, in seventeen sixty-four, King George the Third settled a longstanding border dispute by ruling that the Connecticut River was the boundary of New York, placing the entire New Hampshire Grants under the jurisdiction of the Royal Colony of New York. Wealthy New York land speculators and politicians in Albany immediately began re-granting the very same land to their aristocratic cronies, ordering the established settlers to either repurchase their homes at extortionate prices or face immediate eviction by New York sheriffs.
Furious at this legal robbery, the settlers refused to submit. United by a fierce Appalachian frontier ethos, they organized local committees of safety and formed the Green Mountain Boys to physically resist New York jurisdiction. By the time the American Revolution erupted in seventeen seventy-five, the people of the Grants found themselves waging a two-front war: defending their northern frontier against British redcoats from Canada while fighting off legal and physical annexation by the State of New York. Pioneer families had cleared ancient virgin hardwood forests with crosscut saws and oxen, investing years of grueling frontier sweat equity into establishing stone walls, orchards, and homesteads.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE DECLARATION OF WINDSOR: A NATION IS BORN
Following the outbreak of the Revolutionary War, leaders of the Grants repeatedly petitioned the Continental Congress in Philadelphia to be recognized as an independent state and admitted into the American confederation. But every petition was aggressively blocked by the influential New York delegation, which insisted that Vermont was sovereign New York territory and threatened to withdraw from the Revolutionary War effort if Congress recognized the rebellious mountaineers.
Realizing that the thirteen united colonies would not protect them, seventy-two delegates from across the Green Mountains convened at Elijah West's tavern in Windsor on July second, seventeen seventy-seven. In a bold declaration of sovereignty, they proclaimed the establishment of a free, independent commonwealth, initially christened 'New Connecticut,' before formally adopting the French-derived name 'Vermont'—meaning 'Green Mountains'—suggested by the eccentric physician and philosopher Dr. Thomas Young of Philadelphia.
While delegates were debating the new constitution, an express courier arrived on July eighth with terrifying news: British General John Burgoyne had recaptured Fort Ticonderoga and was marching an invading army of eight thousand British, German, and Indigenous soldiers directly toward Vermont. As a fierce thunderstorm raged outside, delegates were preparing to abandon the convention to defend their families. Tradition holds that convention president Joseph Marsh ordered the tavern doors locked, insisting they must finish framing the constitution before picking up their muskets. Delegates pledged their sacred honor to defend the new republic against all imperial and colonial aggressors, forging a bond of mountain solidarity that defied both the British Crown and Continental Congress.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE RADICAL CONSTITUTION OF 1777
The Constitution of the Republic of Vermont, adopted during that stormy July convention in seventeen seventy-seven, was not merely an administrative framework; it was the most radically democratic and morally visionary governing charter of the eighteenth century. Drawing inspiration from the radical democratic ideas of Thomas Paine, Vermont's founders established a unicameral legislature—the House of Representatives—directly elected every year by the people, deliberately rejecting an aristocratic upper senate.
Most monumentally, Chapter One, Article One of the Vermont Constitution made history by enacting the first complete constitutional prohibition of adult slavery in the Western Hemisphere. The article declared that no male person over the age of twenty-one and no female over eighteen could be held in bondage as a slave or servant within the republic, striking a historic moral blow against human bondage eighty-six years before Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.
Furthermore, the Vermont Constitution abolished property ownership requirements for voting, establishing universal manhood suffrage for all freemen who took the Freeman's Oath, regardless of wealth or land ownership. It mandated government-funded public schools in every town and a state university, prohibited religious tests for officeholding, and explicitly recognized the right of citizens to hunt and fish on uncultivated lands. It was a constitution built for and by common frontier workingmen. By establishing the sacred principle that every person possessed natural sovereignty over their own body, Vermont placed itself at the vanguard of global abolitionism decades ahead of other nations.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE BATTLE OF BENNINGTON: SAVING THE REVOLUTION
Just one month after declaring independence, the fledgling Republic of Vermont proved its military mettle in one of the most critical turning points of the American Revolution: the Battle of Bennington. In August seventeen seventy-seven, British General John Burgoyne, advancing toward Albany, found his army running desperately short of food, horses, and wagons. He dispatched a force of over eight hundred German Brunswick dragoons, British regulars, and Loyalists under Lieutenant Colonel Friedrich Baum to march on Bennington and seize the massive supply depot gathered there by the Vermont republic.
Vermont Governor Thomas Chittenden immediately sent desperate appeals to New Hampshire, which dispatched veteran Indian fighter General John Stark with twelve hundred New Hampshire militia. Uniting with Seth Warner's Green Mountain Boys, Stark attacked the entrenched German and British forces on August sixteenth, seventeen seventy-seven, famously declaring before the charge: 'There, my boys, are your enemies, the redcoats and Tories! You must beat them, or Molly Stark sleeps a widow tonight!'
In a day of brutal, close-quarters combat fought in suffocating summer heat, the Vermont and New Hampshire militia completely annihilated Baum's column, capturing over seven hundred prisoners, four brass cannons, and hundreds of muskets. The decisive American victory at Bennington crippled Burgoyne's invading army, depriving him of food and transport and leading directly to his historic surrender at Saratoga two months later, which persuaded France to enter the war as an American ally. The resounding American victory at Bennington broke the back of British northern strategy, providing the psychological turning point that convinced European monarchies that the American cause could prevail.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE HALDIMAND NEGOTIATIONS: THE SECRET GAME OF POKER
Despite their heroic contributions at Bennington, the Continental Congress in Philadelphia continued to deny Vermont statehood, caving to relentless pressure from New York and New Hampshire. Facing a hostile British army in Canada to the north and hostile neighboring states to the south and east, Vermont's leaders found themselves in a terrifying geopolitical vise.
Between seventeen eighty and seventeen eighty-three, Ethan Allen, his brother Ira Allen, and Governor Thomas Chittenden embarked on one of the most daring, audacious, and morally ambiguous diplomatic tightrope walks in American history: the Haldimand Negotiations. Secretly contacting General Frederick Haldimand, the British Governor General of Canada, the Allen brothers initiated private talks exploring the possibility of Vermont rejoining the British Empire as a self-governing Canadian province.
In truth, the crafty Vermonters were playing a brilliant, high-stakes game of geopolitical poker. By dangling the possibility of reunion with the British Crown, they kept British forces in Canada from invading and ravaging Vermont's exposed northern frontier, while simultaneously terrifying the Continental Congress with the nightmare scenario of an armed, hostile British enclave on the northern border of New York. The negotiations were prolonged with endless delays and diplomatic double-talk until the Treaty of Paris formally ended the Revolutionary War in seventeen eighty-three, leaving Vermont entirely independent and unmolested. The secret diplomacy kept thousands of British troops idle in Canadian winter garrisons, neutralizing an entire army without expending a single ounce of precious gunpowder or shedding a drop of blood.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SOVEREIGN REPUBLIC IN FULL BLOOM
Following the Revolutionary War, the Republic of Vermont functioned as an entirely sovereign, independent nation for nearly a decade. Governed with steady, grandfatherly wisdom by Thomas Chittenden—a plain-spoken, one-eyed farmer who was elected governor for eighteen terms—the mountain republic flourished outside the dysfunction of the newly formed United States under the Articles of Confederation.
Vermont established its own national post office system in seventeen eighty-four, appointing Anthony Haswell as Postmaster General and issuing official postmarks. In seventeen eighty-five, the Vermont General Assembly granted Reuben Harmon Jr. of Rupert the exclusive right to mint national copper coinage. Harmon established a water-powered mint that struck hundreds of thousands of beautiful copper coins bearing the Latin motto 'Vermontis. Res. Publica'—The Republic of Vermont—along with thirteen mountain peaks rising beneath a smiling sun.
Because Vermont owed no war debt to the Continental Congress, it had no crushing state debt, allowing the republic to offer rock-bottom property taxes and cheap land grants to thousands of settlers fleeing high taxes in Massachusetts and Connecticut. Vermont expanded its borders through annexation, absorbing towns in New Hampshire and New York that voluntarily voted to join the prosperous, low-tax mountain republic. Reuben Harmon's water-powered coin press struck copper planchets featuring the smiling sun rising over the Green Mountains, creating tangible physical tokens of frontier national independence.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: STATEHOOD AND THE FOURTEENTH STAR
By the late seventeen eighties, the political dynamics of North America shifted dramatically. With the ratification of the United States Constitution in seventeen eighty-eight and the establishment of a strong federal government under President George Washington, the leaders of both the United States and Vermont recognized that continuing independence was mutually disadvantageous. For the United States, an independent, sovereign nation on its northern border remained a security liability; for Vermont, access to international trade through New York ports was vital for economic growth.
Furthermore, a critical balance-of-power calculation emerged in Congress. With Kentucky preparing to enter the Union as a Southern slave state, Northern representatives desperately sought a free, anti-slavery state to maintain the equal balance of power in the United States Senate. In seventeen ninety, Alexander Hamilton and New York political leaders finally made peace with Vermont, agreeing to relinquish all colonial territorial claims in exchange for thirty thousand Spanish silver dollars paid by Vermont to compensate New York claimants.
On March fourth, seventeen ninety-one, President George Washington signed the act of Congress formally admitting Vermont as the fourteenth state—the first state admitted to the Union after the original thirteen. For fourteen years, the mountain republic had stood alone, demonstrating to the world that an armed, literate citizenry governed by principles of natural liberty, universal suffrage, and racial justice could create an enduring civilization in the wilderness. Today, Vermonters still proudly carry that fierce, independent spirit, remembering the fourteen years when their mountain valleys formed a sovereign nation under the sun. The admission of Vermont as the fourteenth state established the vital constitutional precedent for admitting new states on an equal footing with the original thirteen founding commonwealths.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Republic of Vermont proved that a free, literate citizenry could govern itself and strike the first constitutional blow against human bondage. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we travel to Portsmouth, New Hampshire, for Theodore Roosevelt's historic peace conference.
